question: If I'm held in jail awaiting trial, how long can I be held before I must be indicted and tried, and what happens if that deadline passes?

negative: brought to trial within five years

gold_sections.why: The core clock and remedy: dismissal unless good cause is shown when no information is filed within 15 days of being held to answer, a felony is not tried within 60 days of arraignment on the indictment or information, or a misdemeanor is not tried within 30 days (in custody) or 45 days (otherwise); general waivers, request or consent (express or implied) to a later date (trial on that date or within 10 days after), and the rule that an unrepresented defendant is not deemed to consent unless advised.

The pre-charging clock for felony complaints: preliminary examination within 10 court days of arraignment or plea; dismissal for an in-custody defendant held 10 or more court days solely on the complaint unless personally waived or good cause; release under 1318 when set past 10 court days unless the defendant requested the delay or another listed exception applies; absolute 60-day limit unless personally waived.
What a dismissal does for someone in jail: a defendant in custody must be discharged, bail is exonerated and cash bail refunded.

Whether a dismissed case can be refiled: a felony (or a misdemeanor charged with a felony) is barred only if previously terminated (the two-dismissal rule), with the 1387(a)(1)-(4) exceptions (substantial new evidence, direct witness intimidation, certain spousal-witness failures to appear, contempt) available only in those felony cases; a misdemeanor charged alone is barred after one termination, except the 1387(b) domestic violence witness no-show rule; a prior 859b termination does not count if good cause is shown why the preliminary examination was not held within 60 days (1387(c)).
Alternative to dismissal: where sufficient reason is shown, the court may continue the action and meanwhile may discharge the defendant from custody on his or her own undertaking.

The first clock: an arrested defendant must be taken before a magistrate without unnecessary delay and within 48 hours, excluding Sundays and holidays, extended to the next court session when the time expires while court is not in session.
The district attorney's duty to file the information within 15 days after the defendant is examined and committed (held to answer).
In felony cases the court must set a trial date within 60 days of arraignment in superior court unless it finds good cause under 1050 and states the facts on the record.

Continuances: only on a showing of good cause (not mere convenience or stipulation), written notice two court days ahead, findings on the record; the prosecutor's other trial is good cause in listed case types for at most 10 more court days; the section itself is directory and does not mandate dismissal.

The defendant's immediate remedy when a magistrate sets the preliminary examination beyond the 859b limit or continues it without required good cause: a petition for writ of mandate or prohibition with precedence over all other cases.

In-code ceiling during court emergencies: on the Chairperson of the Judicial Council's order, the 859b deadline can be extended to at most 15 court days, the 1382 trial deadline by at most 30 days (in-custody trials get precedence), and in a proclaimed disaster emergency the 825 48-hour limit to at most seven days for felonies.
For a violent felony dismissed twice, the prosecution gets one more refiling if a prior dismissal was due solely to excusable neglect (never for bad faith).
With both sides' express consent the court may proceed on the existing pleading instead of dismissing; it counts as a prior termination and a new 859b or 1382 period starts on rearraignment.

nuggets.text: An arrested defendant must be taken before a magistrate without unnecessary delay and within 48 hours of arrest, excluding Sundays and holidays; if the 48 hours run out while court is not in session, the time extends through the next court session on the following judicial day.
nuggets.quote: the defendant shall in all cases be taken before the magistrate without unnecessary delay, and, in any event, within 48 hours after his or her arrest, excluding Sundays and holidays. (2) When the 48 hours prescribed by paragraph (1) expire at a time when the court in which the magistrate is sitting is not in session, that time shall be extended to include the duration of the next court session on the judicial day immediately following.

nuggets.text: On a felony complaint, the preliminary examination must be held within 10 court days of arraignment or plea, whichever is later, unless both sides waive that right or good cause for a continuance is found under 1050.
nuggets.quote: unless both waive that right or good cause for a continuance is found as provided for in Section 1050, the preliminary examination shall be held within 10 court days of the date the defendant is arraigned or pleads, whichever occurs later

nuggets.text: If the defendant is in custody, the magistrate must dismiss the complaint when the preliminary examination is set or continued beyond 10 court days and the defendant has remained in custody 10 or more court days solely on that complaint, unless the defendant personally waives the preliminary examination within the 10 court days or the prosecution establishes good cause for a continuance.
nuggets.quote: the magistrate shall dismiss the complaint if the preliminary examination is set or continued beyond 10 court days from the time of the arraignment, plea, or reinstatement of criminal proceedings pursuant to Chapter 6 (commencing with Section 1367) of Title 10 of Part 2, and the defendant has remained in custody for 10 or more court days solely on that complaint, unless either of the following occur: (a) The defendant personally waives his or her right to preliminary examination within the 10 court days. (b) The prosecution establishes good cause for a continuance beyond the 10-court-day period.

nuggets.text: If the preliminary examination is set or continued past 10 court days, the defendant must be released under 1318 (own recognizance) unless the defendant requested the delay, is charged with a capital offense where proof is evident, made a needed witness unavailable, or the delay is due to counsel's illness, counsel's unexpected jury trial, or an unforeseen conflict requiring new counsel.
nuggets.quote: If the preliminary examination is set or continued beyond the 10-court-day period, the defendant shall be released pursuant to Section 1318 unless: (1) The defendant requests the setting of continuance of the preliminary examination beyond the 10-court-day period.

nuggets.text: The magistrate must dismiss the complaint if the preliminary examination is set or continued more than 60 days from arraignment or plea, unless the defendant personally waives the preliminary examination within the 60 days.
nuggets.quote: The magistrate shall dismiss the complaint if the preliminary examination is set or continued more than 60 days from the date of the arraignment, plea, or reinstatement of criminal proceedings pursuant to Chapter 6 (commencing with Section 1367) of Title 10 of Part 2, unless the defendant personally waives his or her right to a preliminary examination within the 60 days.

nuggets.text: Unless good cause to the contrary is shown, the court must order the action dismissed when the 1382 deadlines are missed.
nuggets.quote: The court, unless good cause to the contrary is shown, shall order the action to be dismissed in the following cases

nuggets.text: After a person is held to answer (after the preliminary examination), the case must be dismissed if no information is filed within 15 days.
nuggets.quote: When a person has been held to answer for a public offense and an information is not filed against that person within 15 days.

nuggets.text: In a felony case, the defendant must be brought to trial within 60 days of arraignment on the indictment or information (or of reinstatement of proceedings after a competency suspension); there is no separate deadline to obtain the indictment itself.
nuggets.quote: In a felony case, when a defendant is not brought to trial within 60 days of the defendant's arraignment on an indictment or information

nuggets.text: A misdemeanor or infraction must be brought to trial within 30 days after arraignment or plea (whichever is later) if the defendant is in custody then, or within 45 days in all other cases.
nuggets.quote: when a defendant in a misdemeanor or infraction case is not brought to trial within 30 days after he or she is arraigned or enters his or her plea, whichever occurs later, if the defendant is in custody at the time of arraignment or plea, whichever occurs later, or in all other cases, within 45 days after the defendant's arraignment or entry of the plea, whichever occurs later

nuggets.text: A felony case is not dismissed if the defendant entered a general time waiver; the waiver lets the court set or continue trial without dismissal (withdrawing it in open court restarts a 60-day clock).
nuggets.quote: A general waiver of the 60-day trial requirement entitles the superior court to set or continue a trial date without the sanction of dismissal should the case fail to proceed on the date set for trial.

nuggets.text: If, without a general waiver, the defendant requests or consents, expressly or impliedly, to a trial date beyond the deadline, trial must happen on that date or within 10 days after it.
nuggets.quote: Whenever a case is set for trial beyond the 60-day period by request or consent, expressed or implied, of the defendant without a general waiver, the defendant shall be brought to trial on the date set for trial or within 10 days thereafter.

nuggets.text: When the case is dismissed, a defendant in custody must be discharged from custody; a defendant on bail has the bail exonerated, and cash deposited instead of bail is refunded.
nuggets.quote: If the judge or magistrate directs the action to be dismissed, the defendant must, if in custody, be discharged therefrom; or if admitted to bail, his bail is exonerated, or money deposited instead of bail must be refunded

nuggets.text: If the defendant is not charged or tried in time but sufficient reason is shown, the court may continue the case and in the meantime may release the defendant from custody on his or her own undertaking.
nuggets.quote: If the defendant is not charged or tried, as provided in Section 1382, and sufficient reason therefor is shown, the court may order the action to be continued from time to time, and in the meantime may discharge the defendant from custody on his or her own undertaking of bail

nuggets.text: A dismissal under 1382 or 859b bars a new prosecution for the same offense if it is a felony (or a misdemeanor charged with a felony) and the action was previously terminated, so a felony can generally be refiled once; a misdemeanor charged alone is barred after a single dismissal.
nuggets.quote: is a bar to any other prosecution for the same offense if it is a felony or if it is a misdemeanor charged together with a felony and the action has been previously terminated pursuant to this chapter, or Section 859b, 861, 871, or 995, or if it is a misdemeanor not charged together with a felony

nuggets.text: The exceptions in 1387(a) apply only in felony cases (or misdemeanors charged with a felony): refiling is allowed if the judge finds substantial new evidence not discoverable with due diligence, termination caused by direct intimidation of a material witness, or (within six months and once per action) a personally subpoenaed spouse complaining witness's failure to appear in listed prosecutions or the complaining witness's contempt.
nuggets.quote: except in those felony cases, or those cases where a misdemeanor is charged with a felony, where subsequent to the dismissal of the felony or misdemeanor the judge or magistrate finds any of the following: (1) That substantial new evidence has been discovered by the prosecution that would not have been known through the exercise of due diligence at, or prior to, the time of termination of the action. (2) That the termination of the action was the result of the direct intimidation of a material witness

nuggets.text: When an emergency (such as war, an epidemic, a natural disaster, public unrest, or a large influx of arrests) threatens a court's operation, the Chairperson of the Judicial Council may by order extend the 859b preliminary examination period from 10 to no more than 15 court days and the 1382 trial period by no more than 30 days, with in-custody trials given precedence.
nuggets.quote: Extend the time period provided in Section 859b of the Penal Code for the holding of a preliminary examination from 10 court days to not more than 15 court days. (10) Extend the time period provided in Section 1382 of the Penal Code within which the trial must be held by not more than 30 days, but the trial of a defendant in custody whose time is so extended shall be given precedence over all other cases.

deadline.anchor: after arrest, excluding Sundays and holidays, extended through the next court session if it expires while court is not in session (first appearance before a magistrate)

after arraignment or plea on a felony complaint, whichever is later (preliminary examination; an in-custody defendant held 10 or more court days solely on that complaint gets dismissal unless personal waiver or good cause)
after arraignment or plea on a felony complaint (outer limit for the preliminary examination unless personally waived)
after the defendant is held to answer (information must be filed)
after arraignment on the indictment or information in a felony case (trial must begin)
after arraignment or plea, whichever is later, in a misdemeanor or infraction case when the defendant is in custody at that time (trial must begin)
after arraignment or plea, whichever is later, in a misdemeanor or infraction case when the defendant is not in custody (trial must begin)
after a trial date the defendant requested or consented to (expressly or impliedly) beyond the statutory period without a general waiver

answer: You must see a judge within 48 hours of arrest, excluding Sundays and holidays (extended if court is closed) [N1]. A felony preliminary hearing is due within 10 court days of arraignment or plea [N2]. If you have been jailed 10 or more court days solely on that complaint and it is set later, the complaint must be dismissed unless you personally waive time or the prosecution shows good cause [N3]. If it is set later, you must be released on your own recognizance unless you asked for the delay or another listed exception applies, like your lawyer's illness [N4]. Past 60 days the complaint must be dismissed unless you waived [N5]. Once held to answer, the information must be filed within 15 days [N7]. Indictment has no separate deadline; felony trial must start within 60 days of arraignment on the indictment or information [N8], misdemeanor trial within 30 days of arraignment or plea if jailed, otherwise 45 [N9]. A general time waiver removes dismissal [N10]; requesting or agreeing to a later date, even implicitly, means trial then or within 10 days [N11]. If a deadline passes, the court must dismiss unless good cause is shown [N6], and you must be released [N12]; with sufficient reason it may instead continue the case and release you on your promise [N13]. A felony dismissed twice, or a stand-alone misdemeanor dismissed once, generally cannot be refiled [N14]; felony exceptions include new evidence or witness intimidation [N15]. Emergency orders can extend these deadlines [N16].

out_of_corpus.what: The constitutional speedy trial right, which applies apart from the statutory deadlines and is judged by a balancing test (length of delay, reason, assertion of the right, prejudice); California's parallel guarantees
out_of_corpus.where: Sixth Amendment to the U.S. Constitution; Barker v. Wingo, 407 U.S. 514 (1972); California Constitution, Article I, Sections 15 and 29

out_of_corpus.what: (Case law and court rules) What counts as 'good cause' to deny dismissal or continue past the deadline (for example, whether chronic court congestion, prosecutor unavailability, or defense counsel's requested delay over the defendant's objection qualifies), and what conduct amounts to implied consent to a later trial date (for example, failing to object when a date past the deadline is set)
out_of_corpus.where: Decisions of the California Supreme Court and Courts of Appeal interpreting Penal Code 1382 and 859b (case law); California Rules of Court governing continuances in criminal cases (rule 4.113)

out_of_corpus.what: (Case law) How the 1387 two-dismissal rule applies when a misdemeanor is refiled as a felony or charges are refiled in a new complaint, and when a dismissal counts as a prior termination
out_of_corpus.where: California case law interpreting Penal Code 1387 (e.g., Burris v. Superior Court, 34 Cal.4th 1012 (2005))

notes: California has no statutory deadline to obtain a grand jury indictment as such; felonies usually proceed by complaint, preliminary examination (859b) and information (1382 (a)(1), 739); a complaint dismissed before the preliminary hearing in favor of an indictment on the same subject matter is not a bar (1387 (c)), and the 60-day trial clock then runs from arraignment on the indictment. 825 (a)(2): if the 48 hours expire while court is in session, arraignment may occur any time during that session; an arrest on a non-holiday Wednesday after the day's session must be brought before the magistrate no later than the following (non-holiday) Friday. The 1382 felony and misdemeanor clocks also restart after a mistrial, a new-trial order, an appellate remittitur, or reinstatement after a competency suspension (proceedings are suspended during a competency inquiry, 1368 (c)); 90 days applies where the district attorney resubmits a case for preliminary examination after a writ or appeal reversing a pre-preliminary-hearing guilty plea. A felony defendant who fails to appear and is arrested on a bench warrant must be tried within 60 days of next appearing in superior court, unless a trial date beyond that 60-day period had already been set (1382 (b)); a misdemeanor defendant who fails to appear is deemed arraigned on the date of the later arraignment on the bench warrant or submission to the court (1382 (a)(3)(C)). Withdrawing a general waiver in open court restarts 60 days (felony) or 30 days (misdemeanor). An unrepresented defendant is not deemed to have consented to a trial date unless the court explained the 1382 rights and the effect of consenting (1382 (c)). 859b allows a good-cause continuance of at most three additional court days in listed child-abuse cases where the prosecutor is in another trial. 861: the preliminary examination must be completed in one session or the complaint dismissed, unless postponed for good cause by affidavit; postponement is limited to 10 court days absent personal waiver or prosecution good cause, an in-custody defendant postponed past 10 court days must be released under 859b, and postponement cannot exceed 60 days from the order unless the defendant consents or moves. 871.6: if the magistrate sets the preliminary examination beyond the 859b limit or continues it without required good cause, either side may petition the superior court for a writ of mandate or prohibition, which has precedence over all other cases. 1050 says continuances require good cause and written notice two court days ahead, but 1050 (l) makes that section directory only; 1050 (g)(2) treats the assigned prosecutor's other trial, preliminary hearing or suppression motion as good cause in murder, stalking, child-abuse, domestic violence, career-criminal and hate-crime cases, for at most 10 additional court days; 1050 (j) requires the court to notify the Chair of the Judicial Council when its calendar may force 1382 dismissals. 1050.1: when jointly charged defendants' cases are continued for good cause, the continuance is good cause, on the prosecutor's motion, to continue the co-defendants' cases to keep them joined. 1049.5 directs felony trial dates within 60 days of superior court arraignment unless good cause is found on the record. 1048 (a) puts in-custody felony prosecutions first on the calendar; 1048 (b) sets a 30-day target for certain victim or witness cases, and 1048 (c) states it creates no statutory right to trial within 30 days. Government Code 68115: besides the 859b (up to 15 court days) and 1382 (up to 30 more days) extensions, (a)(8) lets the Chairperson of the Judicial Council, during a proclaimed state of emergency from a natural or human-made disaster, extend the 825 48-hour limit for a felony defendant to no more than seven days (each authorization lasts 30 days unless renewed), (a)(5) can deem a day on which the court could not conduct 825 proceedings a holiday, and (c) allows renewed extensions up to the paragraph maximums. Time computation (CCP 12, 12a, applying to all codes): exclude the first day and include the last; if the last day is a Saturday or holiday, the period runs to the next day that is not a holiday. 1387: a stand-alone misdemeanor based on domestic violence may be refiled once, within six months, if the dismissal resulted from the failure to appear of a personally subpoenaed complaining witness (1387 (b)); in felony cases the spousal-witness (1387 (a)(3)) and contempt (1387 (a)(4)) exceptions also apply only within six months and once per action; a prior 859b, 861, 871 or 995 termination does not count toward the bar if good cause is shown why the preliminary examination was not held within 60 days, or the 995 motion was granted for listed reasons such as ineffective assistance or a defense-counsel conflict (1387 (c)). Violent felonies get one extra refiling after two dismissals if a prior dismissal was due solely to excusable neglect, never for bad faith (1387.1). With both sides' consent the court may proceed on the existing pleading instead of dismissing, counted as a prior termination with a new 859b or 1382 period (1387.2). The prosecutor may move within 15 days to reinstate a complaint a magistrate dismissed under 859b (871.5). Separate clocks: an in-custody misdemeanor defendant may demand an immediate probable cause determination, continuable at most three court days (991); a person already serving a prison sentence or more than 90 days of county jail may demand trial on other pending charges within 90 days of written notice to the district attorney, or the charge is dismissed (1381; 1381.5 for federal prisoners); the Interstate Agreement on Detainers sets 180 days after a prisoner's request and 120 days after arrival, with dismissal with prejudice (1389, Articles III-V); a detained minor's juvenile petition must be set for hearing within 15 judicial days of the detention order (Welfare and Institutions Code 657).
